clinicalPearls: Characterised by one or a few sharply demarcated round or oval erythematous to violaceous plaques that recur at exactly the same site on each re-exposure to the culprit drug
Lesions favour the lips, genitalia, hands and feet, and may blister centrally before healing with characteristic long-lasting grey-brown post-inflammatory pigmentation
On re-challenge the same patches reactivate rapidly, often within hours, and new lesions may appear with repeated exposures
Common triggers include certain antibiotics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, paracetamol and sedatives, and the same drug reliably reproduces the eruption
The generalised bullous form is a serious variant with widespread blisters and skin detachment that can closely mimic Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
Unlike Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, classic fixed drug eruption usually spares the mucosae extensively and lacks marked systemic toxicity, and recurs at fixed sites
Histology shows interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes and a lichenoid infiltrate, and pigment incontinence accounts for the residual pigmentation
The cornerstone of management is identifying and permanently avoiding the responsible drug, with topical corticosteroids for localised disease and supportive care for extensive bullous forms
reference.pathophysiology: Fixed drug eruption is a localised, drug-specific delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Intraepidermal CD8 memory T lymphocytes persist at previously affected sites after an initial episode; on re-exposure to the drug these resident effector-memory cells are rapidly reactivated and release cytokines that damage basal keratinocytes, producing an interface dermatitis with keratinocyte necrosis. Because the memory T cells remain fixed within the epidermis at earlier sites, the eruption characteristically recurs at precisely the same locations. Melanin released from damaged basal cells is taken up by dermal macrophages (pigment incontinence), explaining the persistent grey-brown pigmentation, and widespread activation produces the generalised bullous variant.
additionalDifferentials: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, especially with the generalised bullous variant
Bullous pemphigoid or other autoimmune blistering disease
additionalInvestigations: Careful drug history correlating exposure timing with lesion onset and recurrence
Skin biopsy showing interface dermatitis, necrotic keratinocytes and pigment incontinence
Patch testing performed at a previously affected site once the lesion has settled
Oral provocation testing under supervision when the culprit is uncertain and confirmation is essential
Assessment of mucosal involvement and skin detachment to gauge severity in bullous cases
Baseline bloods and monitoring for fluid balance in extensive generalised disease
redFlags: Widespread blistering and skin detachment suggesting generalised bullous fixed drug eruption or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction
Significant mucosal involvement raising concern for Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis
Systemic upset, fever or large body-surface involvement
Recurrent episodes indicating continued inadvertent exposure to the culprit drug
reference.prognosis: Localised fixed drug eruption resolves after the drug is stopped, leaving persistent pigmentation but no serious sequelae; the generalised bullous variant carries a more guarded prognosis with a mortality that, although lower than toxic epidermal necrolysis, is not negligible in extensive disease.
pitfalls: Failing to elicit the culprit drug so that repeated re-exposure causes recurrent and potentially more severe episodes
Mistaking the generalised bullous form for Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, or vice versa
Attributing the residual pigmentation to another cause and missing the diagnosis
Overlooking over-the-counter analgesics and sedatives as common triggers
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on cutaneous drug reactions
management: Prompt identification and lifelong avoidance of the culprit drug, which is the definitive intervention
Topical corticosteroids for localised lesions and oral antihistamines for associated pruritus

Management of the generalised bullous variant as for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, with fluid and electrolyte support, wound care and nursing in a high-dependency or burns setting when extensive
Clear documentation of the drug allergy and a patient warning to prevent inadvertent re-exposure and use of cross-reacting agents
Confirmatory patch testing at a previously affected site, or supervised oral provocation, when the culprit is uncertain
Dermatology referral for severe or diagnostically unclear cases
